idiom_name: is-pattern test against per-element visitor interfaces
implementation_notes: The structure is written by hand: an empty marker interface as the degenerate visitor base, one visitor interface per element declaring Visit(TElement), and an Accept override whose body is if (visitor is ICircleVisitor typed) typed.Visit(this); - the type pattern is both the safe test and the cast, and the else branch is the visitor that cannot visit this element. Nothing in the language supplies this acyclic interface family. Modern C# pattern matching (including switch expressions over type or property patterns) is the language-supported alternative for a closed set, where exhaustiveness diagnostics are more useful than independent element releases. Keep the classic IVisitor with one method per element when the element set is stable and you want compile-time coverage.
pitfalls: The marker interface must stay empty: a default Visit implementation on it looks harmless but makes every visitor silently capable of everything and removes the compile-time signal about which elements a visitor supports.

A type pattern against an interface succeeds for any implementer, including a visitor that implements the interface for an unrelated reason, so overload the interface with a distinct name per element rather than reusing a generic one.

Mixing as and is - as returning null and is binding a variable - is how a failed test turns into a NullReferenceException or an InvalidCastException; pick the type pattern and keep the failure branch explicit.
